title: America's Most Hated
narrativeQuestion: Who were Americans told to boo, and why then?

chapters.title: The Man Who Sold the Villains
chapters.claim: Episode 1 of Mr. McMahon shows a promoter choosing the Iron Sheik because the hostage crisis made Americans want to see an Iranian lose.

namedPeople.name: Vince McMahon
namedPeople.note: Seen in the embedded Netflix trailer; no still reproduced.

chapters.title: How Fast Did Wrestling Answer the News?
chapters.claim: Three of four major foreign heels arrived within two months of the headline they borrowed; the Iron Sheik shows a character reshaped rather than created.

namedPeople.name: Hulk Hogan
namedPeople.note: Appears in the embedded WWE match video.

chapters.title: A Heel Is a Role, Not a Person
chapters.claim: The same men switched between heel and face as the news and their opponents changed.

namedPeople.name: Jack Swagger
namedPeople.note: No free period photograph; a typographic We the People panel carries the 2013 catchphrase instead.

chapters.title: Fifteen Heels, One Each
chapters.claim: Most villains sold as outsiders were played by men from somewhere else, and the card's fears cluster around Russia and the Middle East.

chapters.title: Pick One Heel. Investigate Two Stories.
chapters.claim: Sixty of the hundred points come from the history behind the character.

chapters.title: Prove the Connection With Dates
chapters.claim: Ordering the hostage crisis and the Iron Sheik's title run shows an event can reshape a character without creating it.

chapters.title: What You Turn In
chapters.claim: The project requires two credible sources, one visual, three slides and no repeated slurs.

chapters.title: The Question We End On
chapters.claim: Wrestling companies taught audiences who the villains were supposed to be.

accuracyNotes: The Iron Sheik worked as an Iranian heel before November 1979; the hub says the crisis reshaped the character.
WWE claimed WrestleMania VII moved for security reasons; WWE acknowledged in 2024 the cause was ticket sales.
Rusev's Putin dedication is dated to a May 14, 2014 Daily Beast report, so the 57 day gap is a measured upper bound.
The 1979 protest photograph contains an ethnic slur; it is captioned as evidence of prejudice, never quoted.
